name: The Michelson-Morley Experiment
statement: The famous failed search for the aether found no change in the speed of light whichever way the Earth moved.
statementAccent: found no change in the speed of light whichever way the Earth moved
meaning: The Michelson-Morley experiment was a landmark physics experiment performed by Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley in 1887 in Cleveland, Ohio, at what is now Case Western Reserve University, designed to detect the motion of the Earth through the luminiferous aether. In the nineteenth century, light was thought to travel through an invisible medium filling all space, the aether, and if the Earth moved through this medium, the speed of light measured on Earth should differ slightly depending on whether the light travelled along the direction of the Earth's motion or across it. Using a highly sensitive instrument called an interferometer, which splits a beam of light into two perpendicular paths and recombines them to reveal tiny differences in travel time as a shift in interference fringes, Michelson and Morley searched for this difference. They found none: the speed of light was the same in all directions, a null result. This famous failed experiment cast grave doubt on the existence of the aether and became one of the key pieces of evidence pointing toward the constancy of the speed of light, a cornerstone of Einstein's special theory of relativity in 1905.
mechanism: The experiment used an interferometer to compare the speed of light along two perpendicular directions with extreme precision. A beam of light struck a half-silvered mirror that split it into two beams travelling at right angles along arms of roughly equal length, effectively about eleven metres each through multiple reflections. Each beam reflected off a mirror at the end of its arm and returned to recombine at the splitter, where the two waves overlapped to form interference fringes. If the Earth were moving through a stationary aether, light travelling along the direction of motion and light travelling across it would take slightly different times, and this difference should shift the fringes. To detect so small an effect, the whole apparatus was mounted on a heavy sandstone slab floating in a trough of mercury so it could be rotated smoothly, and the fringes were watched for any shift as the instrument turned and as the Earth moved through the seasons. The predicted shift never appeared; the measured displacement was a tiny fraction, about one-fortieth, of what the aether theory predicted, consistent with no motion relative to any aether. The speed of light was independent of direction, the null result at the heart of the experiment.

examples.text: The interferometer rested on a sandstone slab floating in mercury so it could be rotated smoothly to compare the speed of light in every direction.
As the apparatus turned, the expected shift in the interference fringes never appeared, giving the famous null result.
The experiment is often called the most famous failed experiment in history, since it found nothing it set out to detect.

variants.name: The null result

whyItMatters: The Michelson-Morley experiment is one of the most important experiments in the history of physics, precisely because it failed to find what it sought. By searching with unprecedented precision for the Earth's motion through the aether and finding nothing, it undermined the nineteenth-century belief in a luminiferous aether as the medium of light and helped clear the way for a revolution in physics. Its null result is a foundational piece of evidence for the constancy of the speed of light, the principle that light travels at the same speed for all observers regardless of their motion, which became a cornerstone of Albert Einstein's special theory of relativity in 1905. The experiment thus marks a turning point between classical and modern physics and stands as the archetype of the fruitful negative result, showing that an experiment that detects nothing can overturn a theory and reshape a science. Michelson's pioneering precision instruments earned him the 1907 Nobel Prize in Physics, the first won by an American in the sciences.

limits: The Michelson-Morley experiment is a precise null result whose interpretation was worked out over the following decades rather than all at once, since Michelson himself first regarded it as a failure for not detecting the aether, and the full theoretical meaning came with special relativity in 1905. A minor historical caveat is that Michelson had performed a cruder solo version in Potsdam around 1880 to 1881, so the celebrated 1887 Cleveland experiment with Morley was a refinement rather than the very first attempt. Later, higher-precision repeats have consistently confirmed the null result, while occasional claims of a small positive aether-drift signal, notably by Dayton Miller in the 1920s, were shown to be statistical artifacts and are not accepted.
misreadings: The Michelson-Morley experiment did not by itself prove special relativity; it gave a null result that undermined the aether and pointed toward the constancy of the speed of light, which relativity later explained. It was not the first attempt, since Michelson ran a cruder version around 1880, so the 1887 experiment was a refinement. And the null result is not overturned by claimed detections of aether drift, which have been shown to be artifacts, so treating the experiment as directly demonstrating relativity, as the sole attempt, or as contradicted by disputed positive results, misreads a foundational and repeatedly confirmed null experiment.
origin: A landmark experiment performed by Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley in 1887 in Cleveland, Ohio, seeking the Earth's motion through the aether; its null result helped point the way to special relativity.
